title: Many languages, one .NET
sub: Compilers, CIL and the shared CLS vocabulary
cards/0/title: You can write for .NET in many languages
cards/0/body:
C#, F#, Visual Basic and others. Each has its own compiler, but they all produce the same thing: CIL and metadata, a description of the classes and methods.

That is why a library written in F# can be called from a C# program without any fuss.
cards/1/body: They look different, but C# and F# produce the same CIL: ldarg.0, ldarg.1, add, ret. We'll see what those lines mean in the next lesson.
cards/2/q: Who decides how code is written: where semicolons go, how a method is declared?
cards/2/explain: Syntax is the compiler's business. The CLR only sees CIL and has no idea which language you wrote in.
cards/2/wrong/1: The CLR receives finished CIL. There are no semicolons in it.
cards/3/body:
Visual Basic checks for overflow by default: its + becomes the CIL instruction add.ovf, an add with a check. If the result doesn't fit in an int, you get an OverflowException.

C# doesn't check by default: the number silently wraps around. The compiler decided what plus means, not the CLR.
cards/3/deep: In C# you turn the check on with the checked keyword or the <CheckForOverflowUnderflow> project property. In VB you turn it off with the "Remove integer overflow checks" option. C# rejects a constant expression like int.MaxValue + 1 at compile time (CS0220), which is why the example uses a variable.
cards/4/q: What does this C# code print with default settings?
cards/4/explain: Without checked, C# doesn't check for overflow: the top bit flips and you get the smallest int.
cards/4/wrong/1: That number doesn't fit in an int. The maximum is 2,147,483,647.
cards/4/wrong/2: That's what Visual Basic would do. C# doesn't check by default.
cards/5/title: The CLS: a shared vocabulary for languages
cards/5/body:
Languages have different features. C# has unsigned numbers like uint, but some .NET languages don't.

So that any language can use a library, there is the CLS, the Common Language Specification: rules for what you may expose publicly. The [CLSCompliant(true)] attribute asks the compiler to check those rules.
cards/6/q: The assembly is marked [assembly: CLSCompliant(true)]. Which line gets a compiler warning?
cards/6/explain: uint is not part of the CLS, and Count is a public property. The private field _hidden is fine: the CLS only covers what is visible outside the assembly.
cards/7/q: A public class has methods Run() and run(). Why is that bad from the CLS point of view?
cards/7/options/0: Visual Basic is case-insensitive and can't tell which one to call
cards/7/options/1: Similar names slow the program down
cards/7/explain: Names that differ only in case break the CLS: for case-insensitive languages they are the same name.
cards/7/wrong/2: The CLR doesn't mind. This is a rule for language interop, not a runtime restriction.
cards/8/q: Match each language to its compiler
cards/8/pairs/3/1: Runs the output of any of them
